readerTitle: Why the fastest teams aren't the ones rushing
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Amazon 주주서한의 의사결정 구분) + 가상 적용 (식료품 체인 운영팀, 주스 바, 앱 스타트업)
insight: 속도는 더 열심히 일해서가 아니라, 결정을 '되돌릴 수 있는가'로 나누고 되돌릴 수 있는 결정을 빨리 내려서 생긴다.
misconception: 빠르게 움직인다는 것은 모든 일을 대충 서두른다는 뜻이고, 신중하게 기다리는 쪽이 항상 더 안전하다.

sources.text: Jeff Bezos, 2015 Letter to Shareholders, Amazon.com (Type 1 / Type 2 decisions, one-way and two-way doors)
Jeff Bezos, 2016 Letter to Shareholders, Amazon.com (high-velocity decisions, about 70% of the information)
식료품 체인, 주스 바, 앱 팀 사례와 학습 횟수 차트는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Type 1/Type 2, one-way/two-way door 구분은 2015년 주주서한(2016년 4월 공개)에 나옵니다. 카드에는 직접 인용 대신 요약으로 적었습니다. 게시 전 원문 표현을 다시 확인하세요.
'원하는 정보의 약 70%로 결정하라'는 2016년 주주서한(2017년 4월 공개)의 내용입니다. 카드에는 'about 70%'로 요약했습니다. 원문 확인 필요.
차트 계산: 한 분기 약 13주. 매주 테스트하면 약 12회(첫 주 준비 가정), 승인에 6주가 걸리면 13 ÷ 6 ≈ 2회. 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: Why the fastest teams aren't the ones rushing
body: In his letter to shareholders for 2015, Amazon's founder Jeff Bezos flagged a danger that grows with success. It wasn't bad decisions. It was slow ones.
As companies grow, he warned, they start treating almost every decision as if it could never be undone. Everything gets the same heavy process. And everything slows down.

image.label: Two doors, one marked with a one-way arrow, one with a two-way arrow
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 복도에 문 두 개. 왼쪽 문 위에는 한쪽 방향 화살표, 오른쪽 문 위에는 양방향 화살표. 오른쪽 문 앞에서 사람이 가볍게 걸어 들어가고, 왼쪽 문 앞에서는 사람이 멈춰 서서 생각 중. 실제 기업 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A new shelf layout, stuck in approval.
body: You lead the operations team at a grocery chain with 40 stores. You think a new layout for the snack aisle will lift sales. Head office approval usually takes six weeks.
What do you do?

options.text: Wait for full approval and a complete sales analysis
options.feedback: Safe and by the book. But you spend six weeks learning nothing, and the analysis can only guess what real shoppers will do.

options.text: Try it in one store next week, with a plan to switch back in an hour
options.feedback: You get real results fast, and a bad outcome costs one aisle for one week. You trade a little formality for a lot of learning.

options.text: Roll it out to all 40 stores now to save time
options.feedback: Fast, but if the layout hurts sales, you've hurt it 40 times. Speed on a decision that's costly to undo isn't speed. It's a gamble.

cards.title: Two kinds of doors.
body: Bezos split decisions into two types. Some are **one-way doors**: hard or impossible to reverse. Walk through, and you can't come back. These deserve slow, careful thought.
Most decisions are **two-way doors**. If you don't like what's on the other side, you walk back. These should be made quickly, by small groups or even one person.
His warning: big organizations tend to use the one-way-door process for everything.

cards.title: Speed comes from sorting decisions
body: In early execution, **speed** isn't about working longer hours. It's about how many times you can try something, see what happens and adjust.
The trick is to sort first. Ask: *if this goes wrong, how hard is it to undo?* Easy to undo? Decide today. Hard to undo? Slow down and think.
The grocery test in one store was a two-way door. Rolling out to 40 stores at once was much closer to a one-way door.

image.label: Decision sorting: easy to undo goes fast, hard to undo goes slow
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 가운데 깔때기 위에 "If it goes wrong, how hard to undo?". 왼쪽 출구 "Easy → decide today"(빠른 화살표), 오른쪽 출구 "Hard → slow down"(천천히 걷는 아이콘). 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Slow decisions cost you tries.
body: Two teams, one quarter of about 13 weeks. One tests a new idea every week. The other needs six weeks of approval per test.
Neither team is smarter. One simply gets six times as many chances to learn. Bezos made a similar point: most decisions can be made with about 70% of the information you wish you had.

cards.title: Founders often get it backwards.
body: A new juice bar owner might spend weeks agonizing over the menu board, then sign a ten-year lease after one visit.
The menu is a two-way door. Chalk a new flavor on the board and see if it sells by Friday. The lease is a one-way door. That's where the extra week of thinking pays off.
Speed means moving fast on the first and slowly on the second.

cards.title: Some doors only look two-way.
body: A price cut can be reversed on paper, but customers remember the lower price. A rude reply to a customer can't be unsent. Safety, legal promises and letting people go are rarely easy to undo.
Speed also needs a way to learn. Changing things every week without measuring the result is just motion.
When in doubt, make a decision more reversible first: smaller batch, one location, a short trial.

cards.title: Now it's an app team.
body: Your small software team has three decisions this week: new wording on the signup button, a new onboarding screen for some users, and moving all customer data to a new database provider, then shutting down the old one.
How do you handle them?

options.text: Decide all three in today's meeting and ship by Friday
options.feedback: Two of these are easy to undo. The data move isn't. If it goes wrong, you could lose users' data and their trust.

options.text: Ship the button and onboarding test now; plan the migration carefully, with a way back
options.feedback: You learn from two quick experiments this week and give the one-way door the time it deserves.

options.text: Run all three through a full review before changing anything
options.feedback: The migration gets proper care, but the button and onboarding test wait weeks for no good reason.

cards.title: Move fast through two-way doors. Slow down at one-way doors.
body: Speed comes from sorting decisions by how hard they are to undo, then deciding the easy ones quickly.
**Try it today:** list the decisions waiting on your desk. Mark each one "easy to undo" or "hard to undo." Make one easy-to-undo decision before lunch.
